batchName: Early Republic: Final Conquest of Italy (290-264 BCE) - Easy Batch 1
chapterName: Early Republic: Final Conquest of Italy (290-264 BCE)

questions.question: What was new about the First Punic War for Rome's armies?
options: It was their first war against a Greek king
It was the first war fought by plebeians
It took them outside Italy for the first time
It was their first fight against the Gauls
questions.explanation: The First Punic War took Roman armies beyond the Italian peninsula for the first time. It began with the fight for Sicily.
questions.sourceQuote: It took Roman armies outside the Italian peninsula for the first time, beginning with the fight for Sicily.

questions.question: Which foreign king did Tarentum call on as its champion against Rome?
questions.explanation: Knowing its army could not match Rome's, Tarentum turned to Pyrrhus, king of Epirus in north-western Greece and Albania. He landed at Tarentum in the winter of 281/280 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: So it looked abroad for a champion and found one in Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, a Greek kingdom in what is now north-western Greece and Albania.

questions.question: Who was appointed dictator to end the crisis of the last plebeian secession?
questions.explanation: Quintus Hortensius was named dictator, a temporary emergency office in Rome. He was himself a plebeian.
questions.sourceQuote: To end the crisis, Rome appointed Quintus Hortensius as dictator.

questions.question: Pyrrhus crossed to Sicily to help Syracuse in its struggle against which power?
questions.explanation: Syracuse, the leading Greek city on Sicily, was fighting Carthage, which controlled much of western Sicily. Carthage was a wealthy trading city in North Africa.
questions.sourceQuote: He came to help Syracuse, the leading Greek city on the island, in its struggle against Carthage.

questions.question: Which battle of 295 BC was the turning point that showed nobody could stop Rome from dominating Italy?
questions.explanation: At Sentinum in Umbria, Rome defeated a combined army of Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians. After that, Rome's domination of Italy looked unstoppable.
questions.sourceQuote: The turning point came in 295 BC at Sentinum, a town in Umbria in north-central Italy.

questions.question: Against which power did Rome go to war in 264 BC?
questions.explanation: In 264 BC Rome went to war with Carthage, beginning the First Punic War. Carthage had once been Rome's ally.
questions.sourceQuote: In 264 BC, the same year, Rome went to war with Carthage, the North African trading power that had once been its ally.

questions.question: What does the name Magna Graecia, given to the Greek cities of southern Italy, mean?
questions.explanation: Magna Graecia means Great Greece, a string of rich Greek cities founded by colonists centuries earlier. Tarentum was the most powerful of them.
questions.sourceQuote: Southern Italy was home to Magna Graecia, or Great Greece, a string of rich Greek cities founded by colonists centuries earlier.

questions.question: What did the lex Hortensia of 287 BC do?
options: Cancelled all debts owed by plebeians
Abolished the office of dictator for good
Gave Roman citizenship to all Italian allies
Made Plebeian Council decisions binding on all
questions.explanation: The law made every decision of the Plebeian Council binding on all citizens, patricians included. In theory, patricians and plebeians now had equal political rights.
questions.sourceQuote: His law, the lex Hortensia, made every decision of the Plebeian Council binding on all citizens, patricians included.

questions.question: Where did Pyrrhus first defeat the Romans in 280 BC?
questions.explanation: Pyrrhus beat the Romans at Heraclea in Lucania in 280 BC. Some of Rome's allies promptly switched sides afterward.
questions.sourceQuote: In 280 BC he defeated the Romans at Heraclea in Lucania, a region of southern Italy.

questions.question: After deciding the war in Italy could not be won, where did Pyrrhus sail in the winter of 275/274 BC?
questions.explanation: Pyrrhus sailed home to Epirus. He left only a small garrison of his soldiers in Tarentum.
questions.sourceQuote: In the winter of 275/274 BC he sailed home to Epirus, leaving only a small garrison of his soldiers in Tarentum.
